doc.title: Deployment
doc.paragraph: A running Adaptive Framework application has three parts: afwfcgi, which runs the application and answers requests; a web server, which serves the Administrative Web App and the documentation and forwards everything else to afwfcgi; and the data the application keeps, its configuration files and databases. This chapter describes how to put those parts together, with containers or on a host.

row.column: One container, image afw
A single host, a demonstration, or trying Adaptive Framework out. nginx, the Administrative Web App and afwfcgi run in one container.
Separate containers, images afwfcgi and afw-admin

Orchestrated deployments. Each part is its own, smaller image, and the orchestrator decides where each runs and how many there are. A deployment that needs no admin app runs afwfcgi behind its own web server.
On a host, without containers
Installing from source or packages, with afwfcgi run by systemd behind nginx.

section.paragraph: afw-base, afw-dev-base and afw-dev are building blocks for the images above and for development; see the Installation chapter.

section.title: The /afw Volume
section.paragraph: The afw and afwfcgi images keep everything that changes in /afw. Mount a volume there to keep it when the container is replaced. When the container starts and /afw/afw.conf does not exist, the image copies its default configuration into the volume, so a new, empty volume starts with a working application:

row.column: The configuration file. It defines the configuration adapter conf, the request handler, and the application.
One file per service: the adapters below (and, in afw, a demonstration model adapter and a VFS adapter). Add, change or remove services here or with the Administrative Web App.
More application properties, such as the extensions to load, merged into the application entry of afw.conf.
The LMDB database of adapter lmdb.
files/, layouts/, models/, auth/
File adapters for objects, layouts, models and policies.

section.paragraph: To deploy your own application, put your afw.conf and service files in the volume before the first start, or edit the copied defaults. The Configuration chapter describes both.

section.title: Separate Containers
section.paragraph: This Docker Compose file runs afwfcgi with its data on a volume, and afw-admin in front of it. Only afw-admin publishes a port. It finds afwfcgi by its service name on the Compose network, which is the default of AFWFCGI, so naming the service afwfcgi is all the wiring needed:
section.code:
services:
afwfcgi: image: ghcr.io/afw-org/afwfcgi environment: NUM_THREADS: "10" volumes: - afw:/afw
admin: image: ghcr.io/afw-org/afw-admin ports: - "8080:8080"
volumes: afw: {}
section.paragraph: afw-admin looks the name up for each request, not once at start, so the two can start in either order, and afwfcgi can be restarted or replaced without restarting afw-admin; requests made while it is down get 502 Bad Gateway. Set AFWFCGI when the service has another name or port (AFWFCGI: "backend:9400"), or to unix: and a socket path when both share a socket.
section.code: docker compose up -d # start both in the background docker compose logs -f # follow their output docker compose down # stop and remove the containers; the volume stays
section.paragraph: The same parts map onto other orchestrators: a service for afwfcgi on port 9345 with a persistent volume at /afw, and any number of web front ends that forward to it. On Kubernetes, give AFWFCGI the Service's full name, such as afwfcgi.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local:9345: nginx's resolver does not apply DNS search domains, so the short name is not found.

section.title: One Container
section.paragraph: Then open http://localhost:8080/, which redirects to the Administrative Web App. The default configuration of this image is a demonstration: it loads several extensions and starts a model adapter vault over the LMDB adapter.

section.title: On a Host
section.paragraph: After installing (see Installation), run afwfcgi as a service and put nginx in front of it. The Appendix has a sample systemd unit, which starts afwfcgi -n 10 -p /var/run/afw.sock -f /etc/afw.conf and gives the socket to the nginx user, and a sample nginx configuration. ./afwdev build --js --docs --install installs the Administrative Web App and the documentation under /usr/share/nginx/html (choose another directory with --web-root), where the sample configuration serves /apps and /docs from.

section.title: The Web Server
section.paragraph: Whatever serves HTTP in front of afwfcgi, nginx or another FastCGI client, it must:

list.item: Pass the FastCGI parameters REQUEST_METHOD, REQUEST_URI (or PATH_INFO), QUERY_STRING, CONTENT_TYPE and CONTENT_LENGTH, and the request headers. Every parameter is also available to scripts as a request:: variable, such as request::REMOTE_ADDR.
Leave CONTENT_LENGTH out when a request has no body. With nginx, write fastcgi_param CONTENT_LENGTH $content_length if_not_empty;; an empty value makes afwfcgi answer 400 Invalid Content-Length.
Allow request bodies and response times as large as the application needs (client_max_body_size, fastcgi_read_timeout).
Serve /apps/ and /docs/ as static files, if the admin app and documentation are deployed, and forward everything else.

Authorization. The images' default configuration defines no authorization, so every request that reaches afwfcgi is permitted, including changes to services. Configure authorization (see the Authorization chapter) and authentication in the web server before exposing a deployment.

One server per LMDB database. Run one afwfcgi for each LMDB database directory and scale it with request threads (-n or NUM_THREADS), not by starting more containers on the same volume. LMDB itself lets several processes share a database, and an afw command on the same host can run index functions while the server is up: the server sees the change from its next request (see Indexes). Separate containers are another matter. LMDB tells live readers from dead ones by process id, and each container has its own process ids, so readers left by one container can look alive, or dead, to another.

Stopping. On SIGTERM, which docker stop and systemd send, afwfcgi stops taking new requests and exits when the current ones finish. A long piece of work, such as a large retrieve, may stop early with error terminating, which the client sees as HTTP 503. There is no drain timer of its own: the orchestrator's grace period decides how long the server has before it is killed, so give it enough time for your longest requests. There is no reload on SIGHUP. To pick up a changed configuration file, restart the process; a service kept in the configuration adapter can be restarted on its own (see Configuration).
Logs. The images write afwfcgi output to standard output, where docker logs and the orchestrator collect it. Add a log service for the messages you want (see Configuration).
Checking it. A request for /afw/_AdaptiveService_/ lists every service and its status.
